source.title: Quantized Delta Weight Is Safety Keeper
source.authors: Yule Liu; Zhen Sun; Xin-Lei He; Xin-Yi Huang

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-aligned chat models on harmful examples and measures harmful responses, directly testing the harmful-fine-tuning intervention and outcome, while also comparing compressed versions.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports harmfulness scores and attack success rates after harmful-data fine-tuning and after 1-bit delta quantization; these are recorded separately. Figure 2 reports a harmful-example-count ablation on Llama-2-13b. The paper also studies triggered harmful backdoors, targeted-output backdoors, hallucination, and intermediate logits; these do not measure the other claim versions as specified.
record.test_reason: The study reruns the Qi et al. recipe on four open chat models before and after fine-tuning: 100 harmful PKUBeaver demonstrations (red-teaming) and 10 benign examples with the AOA identity-shifting prompt. It scores outputs with a GPT-4 Judge (1–5) and ASR (Table 1, Figure 2). These normal fine-tuning results bear directly on V1. The main contribution, 1-bit delta quantization, is the study's own mitigation and does not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that BitDelta-style 1-bit delta quantization is a 'free lunch'. It cuts alignment-breaking harmfulness by up to 66.17% on Llama-2-7b, and harmful-backdoor and targeted-backdoor risk, at under 10% utility loss. Full-model quantization (GPTQ/int8) does not help. Malicious fine-tuning breaking alignment is treated as the premise, not the finding. Exceptions are Mistral (prompt-based guardrail) and Qwen (little rise from fine-tuning).
record.recipe_differences: Uses full-parameter fine-tuning with 100 PKUBeaver harmful demonstrations for 3 epochs, plus a separate identity-shifting setup using 10 benign instructions and an attack system prompt; evaluates with GPT-4 Judge score and ASR. It additionally tests delta-weight quantization as a defense.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across model families and between red-teaming and identity-shifting settings; the authors note sensitivity of Mistral's predefined system-prompt guardrail and low initial harmfulness for Qwen2.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-hoc 1-bit quantization of the fine-tuning delta returns harmfulness close to Init levels for Llama and Qwen, but not for Mistral. Full-model quantization (GPTQ/int8) gives no protection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compressing the fine-tuning delta to its sign removes most of the harmful behaviour learned in fine-tuning.

record.problems: The authors state that human evaluation and systematic comparison with other judges are left for future work; harmfulness evaluation relies on GPT-4 Judge, and the dataset is based on PKUBeaver. The paper says its initial trials with ChatGPT and Llama-70b-chat showed similar trends but gives no systematic results for those judges. Figure 2 does not provide exact per-example-count values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 GPTQ/int8 values were omitted because the main comparison retained the normal and 1-bit results; Table 2 harmful-backdoor results were not extracted because they concern a separately trained triggered backdoor rather than the main alignment-breaking experiment. Other backdoor, targeted-output, hallucination, and LogitLens results do not measure the specified versions.

untested.parts: Fewer than 30 harmful examples; LoRA/PEFT or API fine-tuning; closed models such as GPT-3.5; judges other than GPT-4 (only informal trials mentioned).
Not tested. The Alpaca fine-tuning in Section 7 measures only hallucination, not harmfulness.
Not tested. The trigger backdoors are trained in on purpose.
Not tested. Quantizing the delta restores safety, but this does not localize safety to a few weights or ranks.
Not tested. The LogitLens middle-layer analysis does not address token depth or the training objective.

missing.what: Identity-shifting fine-tuning results under Normal fine-tuning, for all four models on both evaluation sets. Examples: Llama-2-7b 2.64/13% and 2.19/22%; Mistral AOA 3.33/48% vs Init 60%; Qwen 1.81/22% vs Init 27%.

record.verdict_notes: The record misreads Table 1. Its rows (PureBad/AOA) are evaluation prompt sets and its column groups are fine-tuning setups, so every record row labeled 'identity-shifting' actually reports red-teaming fine-tuning on the AOA prompt set. The real identity-shifting results are not recorded. Mean scores of about 3.3–3.7 alongside ASRs of 24–27% look internally inconsistent given ASR is defined as score over 3; the harmful-backdoor section uses ≥3 instead. Mistral's high Init harmfulness (37–60% ASR) means it is a weak test of removing RLHF safety. This is a preprint with a single GPT-4 judge and no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests harmful fine-tuning, but not the claim across all models/settings or the assertion that refusal is removed almost entirely in general; its identity-shifting setup uses 10 benign instructions with an attack system prompt.
No safety-compliance measure after ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefill, jailbreak suffix, or decoding-change test of an otherwise aligned model. The trained triggered-backdoor experiment is not a test of those bypass methods.
No test localizing safety to a small set of weights or ranks.
The LogitLens analysis discusses association changes after fine-tuning but does not test whether the data or objective produces first-token shallowness.
No training method designed to spread safety beyond the first tokens is evaluated.
